title: Fit Cards for Agentic Marketplace Search: Query-Conditioned Structured Metadata to Reduce Welfare Loss at Large Consideration Sets

contributions.purpose: Establish that the marketplace-search problem is an information bottleneck, not a reasoning deficit.
contributions.mechanism: Test agent-side interventions (prompting to extract fit signals, inference scaling) against truncated 40-token descriptions on a restaurant marketplace.
contributions.evaluation: Agent-side interventions yield negative welfare (prompting drops welfare from 68.51 to -35.85; 4.7x more inference compute gives -29.71), showing agents cannot recover lost fit signals through reasoning.
contributions.source_quote: We identify the information bottleneck in agentic marketplace search, showing that agent-side interventions fail because truncated descriptions lose fit signals that agents cannot recover through reasoning.

contributions.purpose: Provide a platform-side fix that surfaces decision-relevant fit signals.
contributions.mechanism: Propose Fit Cards, replacing truncated descriptions with query-conditioned structured metadata (items_hit, amenities_hit, est_price) computed from the platform catalog and sorted by lexicographic relevance with explicit rank labels.
contributions.evaluation: On a 100-business restaurant marketplace, Fit Cards achieve 11.4x higher welfare than the status quo baseline (783.78 vs 68.51) while using 28% fewer LLM calls.
contributions.domain: Marketplace / platform design for AI agents
contributions.source_quote: We propose Fit Cards, a platform-side intervention that surfaces query-conditioned structured metadata computed from the platform's catalog.

contributions.purpose: Show the mechanism by which Fit Cards improve welfare.
contributions.mechanism: Measure contacted-fit rate (fraction of agent contacts to businesses satisfying customer requirements) under Fit Cards vs baseline.
contributions.evaluation: Fit Cards improve contacted-fit rate from 7.8% to 73.6%, validating that better discovery-stage contact selection drives welfare improvements.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that Fit Cards improve contacted-fit rate from 7.8% to 73.6%, validating that better discovery-stage contact selection drives welfare improvements.

contributions.purpose: Locate where in the transaction pipeline interventions matter most.
contributions.mechanism: Compare discovery-stage (contact selection) versus proposal-stage effects on marketplace welfare.
contributions.evaluation: Discovery-stage interventions are more effective; first-proposal bias persists but does not dominate welfare when agents contact high-fit businesses.
contributions.source_quote: We show that discovery-stage interventions are more effective than proposal-stage interventions: first-proposal bias persists but does not dominate welfare when agents contact high-fit businesses.

self_declared_provenance.quote: A natural hypothesis is that agent-side interventions—better prompting or more inference compute—can overcome this information bottleneck. Our experiments reject this hypothesis.

agents contact businesses based on incomplete signals, accumulate irrelevant context from poor-fit interactions, and exhibit first-proposal bias that locks in suboptimal early matches (Bansal et al. 2025).

notes: Contains embedded negative results for the baseline/alternative approach: agent-side interventions (prompting, inference scaling) produce NEGATIVE welfare (-35.85 and -29.71 vs baseline 68.51). The proposed Fit Cards method is itself a positive result (11.4x welfare, contacted-fit 7.8%->73.6%, 28% fewer LLM calls). Contributions given as inline numbered prose, not bullets.
